newsitem.title: LEBANON: Syria mediation averts south Lebanon polls battle.
newsitem.headline: Syria mediation averts south Lebanon polls battle.

text.p: Syria has forged a coalition between rival Lebanese guerrilla groups Hizbollah and Amal, preventing a showdown at the ballot box when south Lebanon votes on Sunday in Lebanon's fourth round of parliamentary polls.
Some 8,000 Lebanese troops have been deployed in the south to ensure the security of the polls where voters will choose 23 representatives to the assembly from among 131 candidates.

The groups' leaders, to the surprise of supporters who had expected a hot election battle, on Friday said their candidates will run on a joint ticket after clinching a deal in Damascus, whose 35,000 troops in Lebanon give it a major say.

But it remains to be seen if Amal and Hizbollah rank-and-file and others among south Lebanon's 552,000 mainly-Shi'ite Moslem voters will stick to the uneasy pact and vote for the joint ticket or cross out rival candidates' names.

The militant Hizbollah and the secular Amal fought a bitter war from 1987-90 in south Lebanon for supremacy of Lebanon's 1.3 million Shi'ite Moslems in which 1,300 people died. A pact brokered by Syria and Iran ended the fighting.

Hizbollah, which has eight MPs and four allies in the current 128-seat house, leads a guerrilla war on Israeli occupation forces in south Lebanon. Amal, a civil war militia turned into a political group, also has a guerrilla presence in the south which occasionally attacks the Israelis.
Under the agreement four pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) candidates will run on the 21-member ticket headed by the Syrian-backed Amal chief Nabih Berri, speaker of parliament.
Running against them is a list headed by former speaker Kamel al-Assad and the list of leftist Moslem MP Habib Sadeq.

Under the pact, Hizbollah also gets three candidates and two allies in the eastern Bekaa Valley -- where voting next Sunday will conclude Lebanon's five-stage parliamentary elections -- effectively reducing the representation of the group by one MP.

Two Hizbollah candidates have already lost in the first three rounds of voting in which pro-government candidates won a crushing victory against opposition candidates, including Christian nationalists seeking a political comeback.
But voting so far has been soured by allegations of electoral fraud levelled against the pro-government candidates.
A poll published by Beirut newspapers on Saturday showed that 53 percent of south Lebanon's voters favoured a joint Amal-Hizbollah ticket while 42 percent opposed it.

The two groups, both of whom have good relations with Syria, were allied in the 1992 polls. But news of the pact, leaked to the press before the weekend, disappointed the rival groups' supporters who had expected a fierce battle at the ballot box.

Hizbollah chief Sheikh Hassan Nasrallah was almost apologetic to Hizbollah supporters, telling them at a south Lebanon rally on Friday that the coalition with Amal was favoured by Syria to avert possible clashes during the vote.

"It was not hidden that Syria favoured a coalition...South Lebanon is an area of resistance (against Israeli forces) and a region of fierce competition on the other hand. There are major political streams there," Nasrallah said.

"Our interest was in having various tickets...but the only problem with many tickets and accompanying fierce competition is that it may lead to a problem and a clash," the turbaned cleric told a rally of 30,000 supporters in the town of Nabatiyeh.
He appealed to his supporters to vote for the whole ticket, which includes independents and four government ministers.
